title: Verifier-Assisted Generate→Validate→Repair Reduces LLM NetOps Misconfiguration: A Preregistered Emulation Study
abstract: We report a preregistered, fully autonomous study that evaluated whether a verifier-assisted generate→validate→repair pipeline improves operational correctness of LLM-produced network configurations on emulated vendor-diverse NetOps tasks. We preregistered a paired confirmatory design (Npairs=200) comparing unconstrained generation (baseline) to a verifier-assisted pipeline (guarded) using a single hosted LLM (gpt-5-mini) and a deterministic emulation-based oracle validator. All experimental artifacts, prompts, validators, and results were recorded immutably. Contrary to the preregistered hypothesis (≥30% relative improvement), both baseline and guarded conditions produced oracle-passing configurations for all 200 paired tasks (baseline_rate=1.00, guarded_rate=1.00; paired difference=0.00; McNemar two-sided p=1.00). We present the preregistration, experiment design, deterministic execution manifest, and failure- and contamination-aware analyses. We interpret the null confirmatory result in light of task construction, shared-generation semantics, validator coverage, and operational scope; we also report exploratory diagnostics and practical lessons for NetOps verifier design and reproducible LLM-for-NetOps evaluation.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs promise to simplify NetOps by translating natural-language intent into device configuration artifacts. However, prior work highlights recurring operational failure modes—hallucinated commands, unsafe ordering, vendor-idiom errors—that limit deployability and motivate guarded generation patterns such as generate→validate→repair and verifier-guided loops [10, 28, 34]. We preregistered and executed an autonomous confirmatory experiment to test the hypothesis that a verifier-assisted generate→validate→repair pipeline increases oracle pass rate relative to unconstrained LLM generation on a set of emulated, vendor-diverse intent→configuration tasks. Our contributions are: (1) a machine-readable preregistration and deterministic execution manifest for paired NetOps evaluation (study-cnd-2026-001); (2) an implementation and public artifact bundle (prompts, validator, task generator, raw outputs, hashes); and (3) the surprising confirmatory outcome (no improvement) together with a diagnostic analysis that clarifies how task design and evaluation semantics influence apparent pipeline benefit.
sections.related_work: Prior work evaluates LLMs for configuration generation, guarded agents, and verifier-augmented workflows. NetConfEval and NetBuddy examine LLMs for intent→configuration translation and emphasize practical failure modes and evaluation challenges [10, 34]. MeshAgent and related systems show that constraint encoding and validator-anchoring improve reliability in production-like NetOps tasks [28]. Recent verifier-grounded workflows (e.g., music StruSpec, Strudel verification) make explicit that executability does not guarantee semantic correctness and that verifier counterexamples enable iterative repair [6]. Our work builds on these threads but differs by (i) preregistering a deterministic paired confirmatory design with an emulation oracle, (ii) freezing generation semantics (shared initial candidate) prior to execution, and (iii) publishing a complete execution and analysis bundle.
sections.methodology: Preregistration. We registered study-cnd-2026-001 before observing any outcomes. Key elements: paired binary design (baseline vs guarded), Npairs=200, protocol buckets (BGP/OSPF/ACL/VLAN), vendor stratification (Cisco/Juniper/Arista), and the primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The preregistration and frozen experiment plan (including seeds, prompts, validator id deterministic_netops_validator_v5, and retry policy) are in the public artifact manifest. Task generation. A deterministic synthetic task generator produced 200 intent→configuration tasks with explicit initial and expected final states and workflow constraints. Tasks intentionally included vendor-idiom and ordering constraints (e.g., "shutdown before MTU change", make-before-break), and varied complexity (simple/complex). Execution semantics. The adapter family hosted_netops_gvr_v1 executed a shared-initial-candidate protocol (both conditions used the same initial generated candidate per pair) as specified in the preregistration. Model and pipeline. All runs used the hosted LLM declared as gpt-5-mini (provider: openai_responses). Baseline: return the model’s generated configuration. Guarded: run the verifier on the model output and—if failing—invoke a single repair call per the preregistered repair prompt. Validator and oracle. A deterministic emulation-based validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) executed the candidate configuration against a containerized device emulator and enforced workflow constraints; validation produced a binary pass/fail and structured counterexamples. Analysis. The preregistered primary analysis used the paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor: paired bootstrap (10k resamples) to infer the paired difference and a McNemar exact two-sided test. Missingness and contamination policies (provider-drift exclusion, oracle-coverage flags) were enforced and logged.
sections.results: Execution and primary confirmatory result. The autonomous pipeline completed all planned calls: planned_episode_count=400, completed_episode_count=400, model_calls_used=200 (shared-initial semantics), and no failed episodes (execution manifest). The primary confirmatory result: Npairs=200 complete pairs; baseline successes=200/200 (1.00); guarded successes=200/200 (1.00); paired difference = 0.00; paired-bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar two-sided p=1.00. The preregistered hypothesis (≥30% relative improvement) was not supported. Deterministic reconciliation confirmed marginal and pair accounting consistency. Exploratory diagnostics. We inspected validator traces, per-task difficulty tags, and repair-iteration fields. For this run the guarded repair path was not exercised because the shared initial candidates already satisfied the oracle in all pairs; therefore no guarded-only repairs occurred. Contamination checks and model-call audits recorded stable provider identifiers and no provider-drift events. All recorded artifacts (raw responses, validator traces, hashes) are available in the artifact bundle.
sections.discussion: Interpretation. The confirmatory null result does not imply that verifier-assisted pipelines cannot improve correctness in general. Instead, three execution-specific factors explain why both conditions passed all oracle checks: (1) shared_initial_generation semantics: both baseline and guarded reused the same initial candidate (the adapter’s shared stage), producing identical artifacts for the two conditions and removing variation that would allow the guarded pipeline to demonstrate improvement; (2) task construction and synthetic oracle scope: tasks were deterministic, constrained, and generated with explicit required sequences that the model often reproduced under the shared-generation policy; and (3) repair budget and policy: preregistration allowed at most one repair call per task, and the repair path was not invoked because the initial candidate passed. These facts are fully captured by our preregistration and execution manifests and explain the observed outcome without post hoc changes. Operational implications. The study highlights the importance of (i) independent-condition generation when estimating guardrail efficacy, (ii) oracle coverage diagnostics to detect tasks that trivially accept many candidates, and (iii) realistic task banks (including adversarial or out-of-distribution cases) to stress repair loops. Limitations (confirmatory vs exploratory). The null confirmatory result is definitive for the exact preregistered design executed: with shared-initial-generation semantics, gpt-5-mini, the deterministic validator used, and the preregistered task bank, guarded generation produced no measurable improvement. Exploratory analyses (not preregistered) examined per-task difficulty metadata and noted that several tasks were labeled "hard" yet still satisfied oracle predicates; this suggests the generator–task coupling produced problems solvable by straightforward step sequences. We therefore recommend future preregistrations vary generation independence and expand failure-mode coverage to better assess verifier benefits.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and autonomously executed a paired NetOps study comparing unconstrained LLM generation to a verifier-assisted generate→validate→repair pipeline. The preregistered confirmatory outcome—no difference—is fully supported by the frozen preregistration and deterministic execution artifacts. The result illustrates that experimental design choices (shared vs independent generation, task construction, oracle coverage, repair budget) can dominate apparent pipeline benefits. We release the full artifact bundle (prompts, validators, raw outputs, and hash manifests) to enable replication and to support future studies that vary these design axes. Careful preregistration and deterministic recording are essential for scientifically valid evaluation of verifier-augmented NetOps workflows.

limitations: Confirmatory scope limited to the exact preregistered design (shared_initial_candidate generation semantics, single model gpt-5-mini, deterministic_netops_validator_v5, task bank of 200 synthetic intent→configuration tasks).
Shared-initial-candidate execution semantics eliminated independent variation between baseline and guarded conditions and therefore prevented the guarded pipeline from exercising repairs in this run.
Synthetic emulated tasks and a deterministic emulator-based oracle do not fully represent production heterogeneity (real devices, live telemetry, run-time faults).
Single-model experiment (gpt-5-mini) limits generality across LLM families and instruction-tuning regimes.
Repair budget was restricted to one repair call per preregistration; richer iterative repair policies remain unexplored.
The oracle enforces the preregistered semantic predicates; oracle blind spots (coverage gaps) are possible and are flagged in the artifact bundle (oracle-coverage-ambiguous).
